rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: ‘They forgot’ means they abandoned what they had been admonished to do; the author glosses this as leaving it unpracticed.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (تركوا ما وعظوا به)

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: The people abandoned what the messengers had called them to.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: (تركوا ما دعاهم إليه الرسل)

rows.speaker: أصحاب اللغة
rows.claim: Forgetting here means abandoning: turning away from something makes it as though it had been forgotten.
rows.anchor: وقال أصحاب اللغة: (وإنما كان النسيان بمعنى الترك؛ لأن التارك للشيء إعراضا قد صيره بمنزلة ما قد نسي)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The opened gates were blessings from heaven and earth, namely favor and joy.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (بركات من السماء والأرض، يريد النعمة والسرور)

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: The opened gates were every kind of good after the hardship they had endured.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: ({أبواب كل شيء} من الخير بعد التفسير الذي كانوا فيه)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: God opened what had been closed to them of good; they mistook their new abundance as deserved and their earlier suffering as no punishment, then punishment suddenly overtook them unaware.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: ({فتحنا عليهم أبواب كل شيء} كان مغلقا عنهم من الخير، {حتى إذا فرحوا بما أوتوا}

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan calls this event a divine plot against the people, swearing by the Kaaba.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: في هذه الآية (مكر بالقوم، ورب الكعبة)

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet said that when God grants people things while they persist in sin, this is divine respite leading them on, and he recited this verse.
rows.anchor: وقال - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: "إذا رأيت الله يعطي على المعاصي فإن ذلك استدراج من الله" ثم تلا هذه الآية

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Taking them during ease intensifies regret at losing safety, health, and varied pleasures for affliction and punishment.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني: (إنما أخذوا في حال الرخاء ليكون أشد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: ‘Mublisūn’ means despairing of every good; Muqatil gives the same explanation.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (آيسون من كل خير)

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: An mublis is one who has despaired and lost hope; the word is also used of someone silent after losing an argument or having no answer.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: (المبلس: اليائس المنقطع رجاؤه

rows.speaker: العجاج
rows.claim: A line by al-ʿAjjāj uses ablasa for a man who could not return an answer.
rows.anchor: قال العجاج: يا صاح هل تعرف رسما مكرسا ... قال نعم أعرفه وأبلسا

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Zajjāj defines mublis as intensely regretful, despairing, and sad.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: (المبلس: الشديد الحسرة اليائس الحزين)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic, iblās can mean despair of escape when destruction arrives, loss of an argument, or perplexity at an affliction; these senses are close.
rows.anchor: يكون بمعنى: اليأس من النجاة عند ورود الهلكة، ويكون بمعنى: انقطاع الحجة

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: The comprehensive wording ‘every thing’ intensifies and enlarges the description, as in ordinary speech that one had everything and every joy at someone's house.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري: (في قوله {أبواب كل شيء} عم وجمع تأكيدا وتشديدا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dābir literally denotes what follows behind, such as the last person in a group.
rows.anchor: الدابر: التابع (¬2) [للشيء من خلفه كالولد للوالد

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth defines dabir as a follower and dabr as the last of a people.
rows.anchor: قال الليث: (الدبر التابع (¬3)]

rows.speaker: أمية بن أبي الصلت
rows.claim: Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt's verse depicts a people being eradicated by a destructive punishment, witnessing the sense of cutting off their end.
rows.anchor: قال أمية بن أبي (¬5) الصلت: فاستؤصلوا بعذاب حص دابرهم

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda takes ‘the dābir of the people’ as their last followers, and cites a line wishing the Al-Muhallab clan's line cut off.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: ({دابر القوم}: آخرهم الذي يدبرهم (¬7)

rows.speaker: الأصمعي وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī and others say dābir means a people's root; cutting it means eliminating their origins so that no trace remains.
rows.anchor: وقال الأصمعي وغيره: (الدابر: الأصل، يقال: قطع الله دابره

rows.speaker: ابن بزرج
rows.claim: Ibn Barzaj says dabir may mean the end of a matter or a man's descendants; the curse seeks to end his lineage so no successor remains.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن بزرج (¬4): (دابر الأمر: آخره. ودابر الرجل: عقبه

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī interprets the dābir of the people as those left behind at the rear of the group; Qutrub gives a similar account.
rows.anchor: فقال الكلبي: ({دابر القوم} غابرهم الذي يتخلف في آخر القوم)

rows.speaker: السدي وابن زيد
rows.claim: Al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd interpret dābir as the people's root: their descendants and others were cut off so none survived.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي وابن زيد: ({دابر القوم}: أصل القوم) (¬10)، والمعنى: قطع خلفهم من نسلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who gloss dābir as ‘root’ connect a people's root to the survival of its descendants; strictly, ‘last/end,’ ‘descendants,’ and ‘root’ are meanings, while ‘last/end’ is the actual explanation here.
rows.anchor: وحقيقة تفسير الدابر الآخر (¬3) والعقب والأصل معنى وليس بتفسير

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: God praises Himself for cutting off the dābir of the wrongdoers and eradicating them completely.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج (¬4): (حمد الله عز وجل نفسه على أن قطع دابرهم واستأصل شأفتهم)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their destruction benefited the messengers whose peoples rejected them; the praise teaches the messengers and believers to thank God for protecting them, and Muhammad and his companions to praise Him for destroying the idolatrous rejectors.
rows.anchor: أن قطع دابرهم نعمة على الرسل الذين أرسل إليهم فكذبوهم، فذكر الحمد هاهنا تعليم لهم ولمن آمن بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb ‘do we call upon?’ may mean seeking success in supplication, as a servant asks God to grant a need, or it may mean worship; commentators take it as worship.
rows.anchor: هاهنا يجوز أن يكون معناه: نطلب النجاح كالعبد إذا دعا الله تعالى بطلب نجاح حاجته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the verse as worshipping beings that cannot benefit us or harm us if we disobey.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يقول: أنعبد {من دون الله} ما ليس عنده لنا منفعة، وإن عصينا لم يكن عنده لنا مضرة)

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The idols own neither benefit nor harm because they are inanimate and incapable of any action.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني: (المعنى: ما لا يملك لنا نفعا ولا ضرا؛ لأنه جماد لا يقدرعلى فعل شيء أصلا)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Returning on one's heels after God's guidance means going back to associating partners with God.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: (أي: نرد وراءنا إلى الشرك بالله)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Arabic describes a person who turns away as returning backward or on his heels.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (ويقال لكل من أدبر: رجع إلى خلف، ورجع على عقبيه)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Zajjāj says the devils made the person love his own desire; on this reading, leading astray is inviting someone into an action through appetite.
rows.anchor: فقال الزجاج: (أي: كالذي زينت له الشياطين هواه)

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda explains istahwathu as the devils drawing the person toward themselves.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة (¬3): ({استهوته الشياطين} استمالته)

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth applies the expression to someone maddened by jinn whom the devils have driven into a state of wandering.
rows.anchor: وقال الليث (¬4): (يقال للمستهام الذي يستهيمه الجن: استهوته الشياطين، فهو حيران هائم)

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Other linguists gloss the verb as seducing and summoning someone into error and following it; Arabs use istahwā of calling someone to misguidance, from a root meaning to desire or hurry toward something.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: ({استهوته الشياطين} بمعنى استغوته ودعته إلى الضلال واستتبعته

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: The root also occurs in Abraham's prayer that people's hearts incline toward his family and settle with them.
rows.anchor: ومنه قوله تعالى: {فاجعل أفئدة من الناس تهوي إليهم} [إبراهيم: 37]

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī derives istahwā from falling from a height, metaphorically applied to straying from the straight path; he compares the forms with azalla/istazalla and ajāba/istajāba.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي الفارسي: (أرى قولهم: استهواه كذا، إنما هو من قولهم: هوى من حالق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority of linguists derive istahwā from hawā yahwī, and Ibn ʿAbbās's wording supports that derivation.
rows.anchor: فأكثر أهل (¬4) اللغة على أن: استهوى من هوى يهوى

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī gives the verb forms ḥāra yaḥāru, ḥīra, and ḥayr; al-Farrāʾ adds ḥayrānan and ḥayrūra.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي (¬2): (يقال: حار يحار حيرة وحيرا)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥayra is wavering without finding a way out or a direction; the word is also used for water that swirls in a cloud or fills a garden and moves about there.
rows.anchor: هي التردد في الأمر لا يهتدي إلى مخرج منه ولا يتوجه له طريق

rows.speaker: لبيد
rows.claim: Labīd's poem describes pools full of water, with the water swirling around their edges.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول لبيد (¬6): حتى تحيرت الدبار كأنها ... زلف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās likens idol worshippers and their callers to a lost traveler tempted by jinn in the desert: following the first callers leads to ruin, while answering those who call to the road leads to safety and guidance.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (هذا مثل ضربه الله للآلهة ومن يدعو إليها

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the parable is of a person who strayed after having been guided.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد (¬3): (هذا مثل من ضل بعد الهدى)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس عن عطاء
rows.claim: In the report from ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the person as ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr, who called his father to unbelief while his father called him to Islam.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: (يعني بهذه الآية: عبد الرحمن (¬4) بن أبي بكر الصديق

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says the devils incited him and he committed sins; ‘confused’ means astray from guidance, and the companions calling him to guidance are his parents and Muhammad's companions.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: (استفزته الشياطين فعمل بالمعاصي {حيران}: ضال عن الهدى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس عن عطاء
rows.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ's report, Abū Bakr answers his son by urging him to follow his own religion and saying that God's religion is the guidance he follows.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: (وأبو بكر يقول: أتبع ديني، ويخبره أن دين الله الهدى الذي هو عليه)

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The passage through ‘come to us’ rebukes a believer for being called to misguidance and idol worship, comparing such a response to a wanderer leaving the clear road.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني: (الآية من أولها إلى قوله {ائتنا} إنكار على من دعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘God's guidance is the guidance’ answers the idol-callers and amounts to ‘do not do that,’ since there is no guidance besides God's.
rows.anchor: لا تفعل (¬4) ذلك؛ لأن {هدى الله هو الهدى}

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq explains three constructions after ‘we were commanded’: with bāʾ, the preposition attaches the command to the act; with bare an, bāʾ is omitted; with li, the phrase gives the purpose for which the command occurred.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق (¬2): (العرب تقول: أمرتك لتفعل، وأن تفعل، وبأن تفعل، فمن قال: بأن تفعل، فالباء للإلصاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading opens both rāʾ and hamza; for readers who otherwise use imāla, loss of the following alif removes the cause for tilting the hamza and thus the rāʾ vowel.
rows.anchor: وهو قراءة العامة، ووجه ذلك أنه الأصل على قراءة من فتحهما إذا لم يلقه ساكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rāʾ is opened here though read with kasra in ‘raʾā kawkaban’ because the reader uses both dialectal forms, treating this rāʾ like the one in ramā and raʿā.
rows.anchor: فتح الراء هاهنا وقد كسره في {رأى كوكبا} فلأنه أخذ باللغتين

rows.speaker: حمزة وعاصم في رواية أبي بكر
rows.claim: Ḥamza and ʿĀṣim in Abū Bakr's transmission read with kasra on rāʾ and fatḥa on hamza; the rāʾ kasra follows the stated underlying analysis and is independent of hamza imāla.
rows.anchor: وهي قراءة حمزة وعاصم في رواية أبي بكر (¬3)، أما كسر الراء فإنما هو للتنزيل

rows.speaker: يحيى بن آدم عن أبي بكر
rows.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Ādam reports Abū Bakr reading both rāʾ and hamza with kasra; the deleted alif remains conceptually present because it was dropped to avoid two adjacent vowelless consonants, like the cited poetic construction.
rows.anchor: وروى يحيى بن (¬4) آدم عن أبي بكر (¬5): {رأى القمر}: بكسر الراء والهمزة معا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story related by al-Suddī, Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, and historians says Abraham left the cave where he was born, reflected on creatures and the heavens, and recognized their creator and provider as his Lord before seeing the star.
rows.anchor: فقال السدي (¬3)، ومحمد بن إسحاق (¬4) # والعلماء بأخبار الماضين: (8) (لما شب إبراهيم في السرب

rows.speaker: السدي ومحمد بن إسحاق والعلماء بأخبار الماضين
rows.claim: In that account, the first celestial body Abraham saw was Jupiter, though another version calls it Venus; he saw it before the moon near the end of the month.
rows.anchor: ثم نظر فإذا المشتري قد طلع، ويقال: الزهرة، وكانت تلك الليلة في آخر الشهر

rows.speaker: أهل التحقيق من العلماء
rows.claim: The verifying scholars reject any account in which Abraham was ever confused or idolatrous: God protected him, he was already a prophet, and the ‘sound heart’ verse means he never associated partners; revelation of the kingdom makes subsequent belief in a star impossible.
rows.anchor: فقال أهل التحقيق من العلماء: (إن إبراهيم عليه السلام لم يكن قط في ضلال وحيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the principal explanation, Abraham said ‘this is my Lord’ to draw his star-worshipping people into the argument, then expose the error of revering stars and assigning them power over events.
rows.anchor: وإنما معنى قوله: {هذا ربي} أن قومه كانوا يعبدون النجوم ويعظمونها ويحكمون بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the star set, Abraham showed its deficiency: a deity should not disappear; he would not take as god something that rises, moves, and passes from place to place.
rows.anchor: أراهم النقص الداخل على النجم بالأفول؛ لأنه ليس [ينبغي] (¬1) [لإله] (¬2) أن يزول ولا أن يغيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second sound interpretation takes Abraham's words as an argument using his people's own assumption: ‘this is my Lord’ means ‘according to you and your claim,’ like God's ironic address to those who imagine partners.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه قال: {هذا ربي} على جهة الاحتجاج على قومه لا على معنى الشك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation supplies an unspoken ‘you say’: Abraham asks his people to say that the star is his Lord, as Arabic and Qur'anic speech often omits the verb ‘say.’
rows.anchor: وجائز أن يكون هاهنا إضمار القول كأنه قال: [تقولون] (¬3): {هذا ربي}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author classifies three sound interpretations: the first is al-Farrāʾ's and chosen by ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim; al-Zajjāj and Ibn al-Anbārī give the second and third.
rows.anchor: فهذه ثلاثة أوجه صحيحة في تأويل الآية، ذكرها أهل المعاني، الوجه الأول: قول الفراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement ‘I do not love those that set’ proves that whatever disappears after appearing is no Lord; alternation between rising and setting shows a created, governed, controlled thing, inconsistent with divinity.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: {لا أحب الآفلين} دلالة على أن ما غاب بعد ظهوره فليس برب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bazagha means that the moon begins to rise; for the sun it is the first appearance of its rising, and stars are likewise called rising.
rows.anchor: يقال: بزغ القمر: إذا ابتدأ في الطلوع

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azharī derives bazagha from splitting: moonlight cleaves the darkness, just as a veterinarian splits an animal's hair at the incision site.
rows.anchor: قال الأزهري (¬6): (كأنه مأخوذ من البزغ، وهو الشق، كأنه يشق بنوره

rows.speaker: الطرماح
rows.claim: Al-Ṭirimmāḥ's line uses bazgh in the veterinarian's sense of making an incision in an animal.
rows.anchor: قال الطرماح: كبزغ البيطر الثقف رهص الكوادن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham considered the moon and sun as he had considered the star, and his argument against his people was the same.
rows.anchor: فإن إبراهيم عليه السلام اعتبر في القمر والشمس مثل ما اعتبر في النجم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's plea for guidance does not imply he lacked guidance; it asks God to keep him firm, as prophets know they could not be guided without God and continually ask Him for this.
rows.anchor: لا يوجب أنه لم يكن مهتديا؛ لأن معناه: لئن لم يثبتني على الهدى

rows.speaker: أبو بكر ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī explains the masculine demonstrative for the sun by construing it as light or radiance; additionally, the word ‘sun’ lacks a feminine marker and resembles a masculine noun in form.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر ابن الأنباري: (إنما قال: هذا والشمس (¬3) مؤنثة؛ لأن الشمس بمعنى: الضياء والنور

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿshā's line uses the masculine verb abqala with feminine arḍ because the noun has no overt feminine marker.
rows.anchor: وأنشد قول الأعشى (¬6): ولا أرض أبقل إبقالها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that ‘this’ means this rising body or this thing through which my Lord is showing Himself to me.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أراد هذا الطالع وهذا الذي أراه ربي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘This is greater’ compares the sun with the stars and the moon; after the argument was directed at his people, Abraham declared his disavowal of their associationism.
rows.anchor: {هذا أكبر} أي: من الكواكب (¬3) والقمر، فلما توجهت الحجة على قومه (¬4) قال: {إني بريء مما تشركون}

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq explains turning one's face to the Creator as directing one's worship and monotheistic devotion to God.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (أي: جعلت قصدي بعبادتي وتوحيدي لله عز وجل)

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ reports Ibn ʿAbbās as taking ‘his descendants’ to mean Abraham's descendants.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس (¬4): (يريد: من ذرية إبراهيم)

rows.speaker: الفراء وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and other scholars take the pronoun in ‘his descendants’ to refer to Noah.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء (¬5) وغيره (¬6): (الهاء في {ذريته} لنوح)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says either antecedent is possible because both Noah and Abraham have been mentioned.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: (كلا القولين جائز؛ لأن ذكرهما جميعا قد جرى)

rows.speaker: علماء النسب
rows.claim: Genealogists prefer Noah as antecedent because Jonah and Lot occur in the listed descendants and are not descendants of Abraham.
rows.anchor: قال العلماء بالنسب: (الأولى (¬8) أن تعود الكناية إلى نوح؛ لأنه ذكر في جملة من عد من (¬9) هذه الذرية يونس ولوط

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read the prophet's name with a doubled lām, al-Laysaʿ; it names the same known prophet, though the single-lām form is more common.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة (¬2) والكسائي (والليسع) بتشديد اللام، والمعنى واحد في أنه اسم لنبي معروف

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says both al-Yasaʿ forms, with doubled or light lām, are used.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: (يقال فيه: اليسع والليسع بتشديد اللام وتخفيفه)

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ considers the doubled form more like foreign names; Arabs rarely attach the article to proper names, though in rare cases it can magnify a name, as in his poetic example.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء (¬4): (والتشديد أشبه بأسماء العجم من الذين يقولون: اليسع ولا تكاد العرب تدخل الألف واللام

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says proper names need no definite article because the name itself identifies its referent; forms such as al-ʿAbbās or al-Ḥārith carry the article when understood as descriptive epithets.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: (الأسماء الأعلام لا تدخل (¬1) عليها الألف واللام، وذلك أن تعليقها على من تعلق عليه وتخصيصها يغني عن الألف واللام

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿshā's line illustrating al-Aḥwaṣ shows that an article-bearing name can be pluralized either as an adjective or as a pure proper name, producing different patterns.
rows.anchor: وقد جمع الأعشى الأمرين في بيت واحد فقال (¬5): أتاني وعيد الحوص من آل جعفر

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says the verse means God guided those already named along with some of their forefathers, descendants, and brothers.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (أي: هدينا هؤلاء الذين ذكرناهم وهدينا بعض آبائهم وذرياتهم وإخوانهم)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: The preposition min is partitive, and guidance is repeated after the long intervening list to restate the main point on which the passage depends.
rows.anchor: فمن هاهنا للتبعيض (¬3)، وأعاد ذكر الهداية في (¬4) قوله: {واجتبيناهم وهديناهم}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the scriptures given to the prophets as the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, the scrolls of Abraham and Moses, and many other revealed books known to God.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يعني: الكتب التي أنزلها الله عليهم التوراة والإنجيل والزبور وصحف إبراهيم وموسى وكتبا أنزلها الله تعالى كثيرة، وهو أعلم بها.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains al-ḥukm as knowledge and jurisprudential understanding.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {والحكم} قال: يعني: العلم والفقه

rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj take ‘if these disbelieve in it’ to mean disbelief in God's signs.
rows.anchor: {فإن يكفر بها} أي: بآياتنا؛ قاله الفراء (¬2) والزجاج (¬3)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وغيره
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and others identify ‘these people’ as the people of Mecca.
rows.anchor: في قول ابن عباس (¬4) وغيره (¬5)

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ's report from Ibn ʿAbbās identifies ‘these people’ as those who rejected the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء عنه: (يريد: الذي كذبوك)

rows.speaker: عبد العزيز بن يحيى
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Yaḥyā reads ‘we entrusted it to a people’ as God preparing and enabling a group for faith, which he takes to show that they were specially created for belief by divine enabling; the wording attributes the act to God rather than them.
rows.anchor: قال عبد العزيز بن يحيى: (يعني: أرصدنا لها قوما وفقناهم لها، وفي هذا دليل على أنهم خلقوا للإيمان بها مخصوصين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك والسدي وابن جريج والكلبي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Suddī, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Kalbī identify the people entrusted with the signs as the Medinan Anṣār; al-Farrāʾ chooses this view.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس (¬2) والضحاك والسدي وابن جريج (¬3)

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ reports Ibn ʿAbbās as identifying the entrusted people as the chosen Emigrants and Anṣār.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء عن ابن عباس: ({وكلنا بها قوما}: اختصصنا بها المهاجرين والأنصار

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda say the entrusted people are the eighteen prophets mentioned earlier.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن (¬7) وقتادة (¬8): (هم الأنبياء الثمانية عشر الذين تقدم ذكرهم)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq prefers that the people are the prophets already named: they believed the revelation brought in their own time, and their patience through rejection and abuse models the Prophet's patience.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول اختيار أبي إسحاق قال: (يعني بذلك: الأنبياء الذي ذكروا

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء
rows.claim: Abū Rajāʾ identifies the entrusted people as angels, a view the author finds unlikely because qawm rarely refers to beings other than humans.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو رجاء: (يعني الملائكة)

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the people as Persians.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: (هم الفرس)

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrī identifies the people as non-Arabs.
rows.anchor: وقال الزهري: (هم العجم)

rows.speaker: أبو روق
rows.claim: Abū Rawq identifies them as learned People of the Book who believed.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو روق: (هم علماء أهل الكتاب الذين آمنوا)

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd includes everyone who did not disbelieve, whether angel, prophet, Companion, or Successor.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: (كل من لم يكفر فهو منهم ملكا كان أو نبيا، ومن الصحابة كان أو من التابعين)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and al-Zajjāj, this verse continues the preceding discussion of the prophets entrusted with revelation; under the other views, it returns to the prophets named earlier.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية متصلة بالأولى على قول الحسن وقتادة والزجاج؛ لأنه في ذكر النبيين الذين تقدم ذكرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ‘those whom God guided’ singles these people out for guidance; if every morally responsible person were guided, the specification would have no point.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله {هدى الله} دليل على أنهم مخصوصون بالهدى؛ لأنه لو هدى جميع المكلفين لم يكن لقوله: {أولئك الذين هدى الله} فائدة وتخصيص

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī explains following their guidance as acting according to their laws and practice.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: (فبشرائعهم وبسنتهم اعمل)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iqtadih linguistically means seeking to make the second person conform to the first person's action.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الاقتداء في (¬6) اللغة: طلب موافقة الثاني للأول في فعله

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says q-d-w is the base from which forms of ‘following as a model’ derive, and qadwa names someone taken as a model.
rows.anchor: قال الليث: (القدو (¬7) أصل البناء الذي [ينشعب] (¬8) منه تصريف

rows.speaker: اللحياني عن الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Liḥyānī transmits from al-Kisāʾī three forms for saying ‘I have a model in you’: qidwa, qidwah, and qidh.
rows.anchor: اللحياني عن الكسائي (¬4): (يقال: لي بك قدوة وقدوة وقدة)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers differ over the final hāʾ in iqtadih: most retain it, vowelless, both in connection and at pause; the more regular rule is to retain it only at pause because it is a pause hāʾ analogous to hamzat al-waṣl.
rows.anchor: واختلف القراء (¬6) في الهاء من قوله: (اقتده)، فالأكثرون أثبتوها في الوصل والوقف ساكنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians prefer pausing after iqtadih because the clause is complete and the hāʾ marks a pause; connecting with it violates the usual deletion of a pause letter, while dropping it in connection departs from the written muṣḥaf.
rows.anchor: والاختيار عند النحويين (¬1) الوقف على قوله (اقتده) لتمام الكلام هاهنا

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī pause with the hāʾ but connect without it.
rows.anchor: وأما حمزة والكسائي فإنهما يقفان بالهاء ويصلان بغير هاء

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī judges the reading of Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī to be the grammatically regular one, although departing from the majority reading feels unsettling despite its agreement with the muṣḥaf.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: (وقول حمزة والكسائي القياس، وفي ترك قول الأكثر ضرب من الاستيحاش
